How start-ups expand into new markets: practical tips for UK businesses

February 13, 2020
Startup Business | Business Tips | Outsourcing

Growing a start-up beyond your home market is one of the fastest ways to raise turnover, and it is also where many young companies stumble. Selling abroad means new customers, new rules and new languages, and each of them needs planning before you spend on ads or stock.

These practical steps show how start-ups expand into new markets, from choosing your first country to making your website, product information and delivery work for customers who do not speak English.

Choose your first export market carefully

Start with one market, not five. Look for a country where there is clear demand for what you sell, where you can handle the legal and logistical side, and where your team can communicate with customers.

The UK government offers free help. GOV.UK has an Export Support Service where you can put practical exporting questions to the Department for Business and Trade, and the government's great.gov.uk site brings together market guidance for UK exporters.

Talk to potential customers before you commit. A handful of conversations will tell you more about price expectations, competitors and language than any desk research.

Sort out the paperwork before you ship

Selling goods abroad brings customs rules, and getting them wrong delays orders and frustrates customers. According to GOV.UK, you may need an EORI number if you move goods between Great Britain and any other country, including the EU.

HMRC guidance covers customs declarations, commodity codes and duties, so read it early and ask your freight partner what they need from you. If you sell services rather than goods, check the rules for the country where your customer is based, as regulated services may need a licence.

Translate and localise what your customers see

People rarely buy from a website they cannot read with confidence. Your website, product pages, checkout, terms and conditions, packaging, instructions and customer emails all need to work in the customer's language.

Translation is only part of the job. Localisation adapts currencies, units, date formats, examples and tone to the market, and it includes the search terms customers actually type. A professional website translation service helps your pages appear in local search results, not just read correctly.

Start with the pages that bring in revenue, such as your home page, top products and checkout, and add the rest as you grow. If your product has safety, legal or technical information, use specialists in legal translation or technical translation, because errors there can cause real harm.

Market in the way your new customers do

Social media and search habits differ from country to country. A platform that works in the UK may not be the main channel in your target market, so check where your customers spend time before you build a campaign.

Partnering with bloggers and influencers whose audience matches yours can be a cost-effective way to reach people, provided they use the local language and follow advertising rules in that country. Slogans and jokes rarely translate word for word, so ask a native copywriter to adapt them. The marketing translation page explains how this works.

Make delivery and returns easy

Customers judge you on delivery as much as on your product. Compare courier and fulfilment partners on price, delivery times, tracking, customs support and returns, and be clear about each of these on your website.

Outsourcing shipping and fulfilment can remove much of the complexity, especially in the first year. Make sure your partner can handle labels and customs forms for your target country, and that the information on your parcels and invoices matches your translated product pages.

Outsource what you cannot do yourself

As your business grows, you cannot do everything alone. Be honest about your strengths and weaknesses, then bring in specialists for the rest, whether that is a freight company, a marketing agency or a translation partner.

Freelancers and agencies let you pay for expertise when you need it, without the cost of a permanent hire. Choose partners with relevant experience, ask for examples of similar work and agree a clear scope before you start.

Test, measure and expand

Treat your first market as a pilot. Track visits, conversion rate, average order value, returns and customer service questions for that country, and compare them with your home market.

If the numbers are healthy, build on that market before you open a second one. If they are not, check whether language, price, delivery or product fit is the problem, and fix it before spending more.

When you are ready to talk to customers in their own language, BeTranslated can help with everything from German and Spanish to Korean. You can find the full list on the languages page, browse the translation services, or request a free quote for your project.

Frequently asked questions

How do start-ups expand into new markets?

Most start-ups begin with one carefully chosen market, test demand with a small launch and then build on what works. You will need to cover legal and customs requirements, adapt your website and product information to the local language and set up delivery and returns.

Do I need an EORI number to sell abroad?

You may need one if you move goods between Great Britain and any other country, including the EU. Check the current GOV.UK guidance or ask your freight partner, as requirements depend on what you ship and where.

Should I translate my whole website at once?

Not necessarily. Start with the pages that drive sales, such as your home page, key products and checkout, then add content as the market grows. Make sure the translated pages are properly optimised for local search.

Where can UK start-ups get help with exporting?

The Department for Business and Trade runs an Export Support Service that answers practical questions from UK businesses, and great.gov.uk provides market information. Your local chamber of commerce may also offer advice.

Is it worth paying for professional translation as a start-up?

Yes, for the content customers rely on, such as product pages, terms and conditions and safety information. A poor translation can damage trust and cause legal problems, while a good one makes your business look credible from the first visit.
